abstract: Highlights • Hepatocellular mTOR-knockout aggravates NASH-associated tumor load. • Histological NASH-scores are lower in mTOR-knockout mice. • mTOR-knockout mice accumulate less visceral fat and have improved glucose tolerance. • Loss of mTOR causes extensive metabolic reprogramming in liver tissue.

2
Materials and methods
2.1
Animals
Animal experiments were approved by the governmental committee (LANUV, Recklinghausen, Germany) and conducted in accordance with the federal German and European law. The experiments were also in compliance with the ARRIVE guidelines and the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (8th edition, NIH publication, 2011, USA). The murine liver epithelial cell-specific (albumin-Cre) mTOR knockout strain (termed mTOR
LEC
) was previously described
[12]
. Mice were bred and housed under SPF conditions according to FELASA guidelines in the animal facility. Due to sex-related differences in manifestation of the metabolic syndrome, female mice were excluded from the analysis.
2.2
Study design
NASH-HCC was induced by application of 7,12-Dimethylbenz[a]anthracene (DMBA; 50 µL 0.5 % in acetone applied to the dorsal surface on the 4th postnatal day) and western diet feeding including sucrose-enriched water (10 %) (adapted from Yoshimoto et al.
[13]
;
Fig. 1
A). Starting at four weeks of age, the animals were fed a diet composed of 40 kcal% fat, 20 kcal% fructose and 2 kcal% cholesterol (western diet; WD; cat# D09100301, Research Diets, Inc., New Brunswick, NJ, USA) ad libitum (mTOR
LEC (DMBA-WD)
and WT
(DMBA-WD)
). Control mice were placed on western diet and treated with acetone (mTOR
LEC (Acetone-WD)
and WT
(Acetone-WD)
) or received standard chow, respectively (SC, V1534-300, sniff GmbH, Germany) (mTOR
LEC (DMBA-SC)
and WT
(DMBA-SC)
; mTOR
LEC (Acetone-SC)
and WT
(Acetone-SC)
). Nine to twelve animals were included per group (Table S1). Body weight and diet intake were assessed weekly. Blood analyses and intraperitoneal glucose tolerance tests were performed every ten weeks. The animals were monitored at least once per week based on a previously described clinical scoring system (Table S2, S3)
[14]
. After 30 weeks of diet feeding, tumor load, liver volume and whole-body fat tissue were determined via
in vivo
non-invasive micro-computed tomography (µCT). The mice were euthanized, the tumor load was macroscopically accessed, and livers and gonadal fad pads were weighted and preserved for further investigation (
Fig. 1
B). Tumor nodules were excised and snap frozen in liquid nitrogen.

2.3
Intraperitoneal glucose tolerance test (IP-GTT)
Mice were fasted for six hours and received intraperitoneal glucose injection after determination of baseline blood glucose levels. Measurements were performed using whole blood from the tail vein (Accu-Chek Aviva, Roche Diabetes Care Deutschland GmbH, Germany) at 0, 30, 90, 120, 150 and 180 min after glucose administration.
2.4
Biochemical analyses
Blood samples were centrifuged in serum gel tubes and serum transaminases (ALT, AST), cholesterol and triglyceride levels were determined.
2.5
Histopathological examination
Median liver lobes were fixed (4 % paraformaldehyde), embedded in paraffin, and 2.5 µm-thick tissue sections were cut. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) as well as reticulin stainings were performed. A pathologist conducted blinded histological assessment and scoring (Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease Score (NAS): steatosis (0-3), lobular inflammation (0-3), and hepatocellular ballooning (0-2); SAF Score: steatosis (0-3), activity (0-4), lobular inflammation (0-2), hepatocyte ballooning (0-2), fibrosis (0-4)). The fibrosis stage was determined according to Kleiner
et al.
[15]
. Sirius red staining was performed to assess the amount of collagen fibers. CD45
+
cells and F4/80
+
macrophages were detected by monoclonal CD45 or F4/80 antibodies (CD45: 14-0451-82, eBioscience
TM
, Austria; F4/80: BM8, 14-4801-82, eBioscience
TM
, Austria). mTOR-activation was analyzed by phospho-pS6 staining (Cat# 5364, CST Europe, Germany). Micrographs were taken at 200x magnification (Olympus BX 43, Olympus Scientific Solutions, Japan) and analyzed using the open-source software ImageJ.
2.6
Micro-computed tomography (µCT)
In vivo
μCT imaging was performed using a dual-energy gantry-based flat-panel µCT scanner (TomoScope 30s Duo, CT Imaging, Erlangen, Germany). Animals were scanned before (fat tissue detection) and immediately after (tumor detection) intravenous injection of Imeron® 400 MCT (BRACCO Imaging, Konstanz, Germany, max. 60 mg/25 g body weight into the tail vein, max. 5 ml/kg BW). The animals were anesthetized using isoflurane. The µCT-scans were performed at 54 kV (0.9 mA), acquiring 1440 projections of size 1944 × 1536 over 9 min of continuous rotation or at 75 kV (120 µA), 2 × 2 detector binning, 1024 projections over 360 degrees, 1.3 times magnification of continuous rotation. After acquisition, volumetric data sets were reconstructed using a modified Feldkamp algorithm with a smooth kernel at an isotropic voxel size of 35 μm. The data were visualized and analyzed with Imalytics Preclinical Software (Gremse-IT, Aachen, Germany) [
16
,
17
]. Fat-containing tissue regions as well as liver tissue and tumors were segmented using an automated method with interactive correction of segmentation errors.
2.7
Tumor scoring
Macroscopically visible tumor nodules were counted during explantation. Diameters were measured and tumor scores were calculated to avoid over-interpretation of small tumors (1-2 mm, score=1; 3-4 mm, score=2; 5-6 mm, score=4; 7-8 mm, score=8; 9-10 mm, score=16; >10 mm, score=32).
2.8
Proteomics
Individual samples were lysed in ice-cold 8 M urea in 50 mM ammoniumbicarbonate (ABC) for 30 min on ice and subjected to 10 sonication cycles (30 sec on/30 sec off). After centrifugation (15 min, 4 °C, 21000g), supernatants were quantified using a bicinchoninic acid assay (Thermo Scientific). 1 mg of each lysate was reduced with 4 mM DTT in 50 mM ABC for 30 min at 56 °C followed by alkylation with 10 mM iodoacetamide in 50 mM ABC for 30 min in the dark. The samples were digested with LysC (1:100 w/w, Wako) in 8 M urea (4 hours, 37 °C) followed by dilution in 3 volumes of 50 mM ABC to yield a 2 M urea solution. Trypsin was added (1:100 w/w, Thermo Scientific) for overnight digestion at 37 °C. Samples were acidified with 10 % formic acid (FA), cleaned using Sep-Pak C18 1 cc Vac Cartridges (Waters) and lyophilized. 100 µg of each sample were subjected to fractionation using a high pH reversed-phase fractionation kit (Thermo Scientific, cat.no. 84868). Eight fractions per sample were generated according to manufacturer's instructions. All fractions were lyophilized, resuspended in 3 % FA/5 % Acetonitril (ACN) and loaded onto a nanoLC system (RSLCnano, Thermo Scientific). Mass spectrometry measurement was performed as described previously
[16]
. Subsequent analyses were conducted on a Q Exactive plus mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific) in data dependent mode (spray settings: spray voltage: 2 kV; capillary temperature: 250 °C). All samples were analyzed on a MS (settings: 70,000 resolution; AGC target, 1e6; maximum injection time, 50 milliseconds; scan range, 350-1600 m/z). dd-MS2 settings were: 17,500 resolution; AGC target: 1e5; maximum injection time: 55 milliseconds; top 20 precursor fragmentation; isolation window, 2.0 m/z; collision energy, 27. dd settings were: minimum AGC, 5e2; 20 second dynamic exclusion; only 2+ to 5+ peptides.
Analysis of raw data was carried out using MaxQuant (1.6.17.0) with the built-in Andromeda search engine
[18]
. The search was conducted against the Mus musculus UniProt database version 12/2020 (reviewed and canonical sequences only) using MaxQuant default settings. Specific settings: Specific protease: Trypsin (two missed cleavages); fixed modification: Carbamidomethylation (Cys); variable modifications: Oxidation (Met) and N-terminal protein acetylation. FDR: 0.01 on both protein and PSM level; minimum peptide length: seven amino acids. Quantification was performed using the MaxQuant label free quantitation algorithm.
The results file was imported into Perseus (version 1.6.14.0). Entries comprised of reversed hits, contaminants, and “only identified by site” were removed. The resulting data were filtered for entries that were identified in all five biological replicates of at least one group. This resulted in 4430 protein groups, where missing values were subjected to imputation using the Perseus default settings and two-sample tests were performed. All proteins fulfilling the requirements (p-value ≤ 0.05, ratio of ≥2-fold change (> 1.30103 (–log (10) p-value), > 2 (log (2) ratio)) were considered significantly regulated. STRING interactions and enrichments analyses were performed using the stringApp (version 1.7.1 (confidence score cutoff 0.40, no additional interactors) on STRING v11) with default values in Cytoscape (version 3.8.2).
2.9
Kinetic metabolic modelling
To simulate the impact of mTOR knockout on central metabolic functions of liver and HCC tissue, we used the kinetic model Hepatokin1
[19]
extended by a molecular-resolved model of hepatic lipid droplet metabolism
[20]
. Briefly, the model comprises all major metabolic pathways of hepatocellular carbohydrate, lipid, and amino acid metabolism as well as key electrophysiological processes at the inner mitochondrial membrane (Supplementary Fig. 1). Enzyme regulation by substrates and allosteric factors are taken into account [
19
,
20
]. Hormone-dependent influences mediated by enzyme phosphorylation were included by a phenomenological model of insulin and glucagon dependent changes of plasma glucose and changes in the phosphorylation state of interconvertible enzymes
[21]
. The maximum activities of enzymes and transporters were scaled using the quantitative proteomics profiles. Simulated changes of plasma glucose level ranged from 5 mM (daytime fasting) to 9 mM (nocturnal nutrient uptake). The model was then used to monitor metabolic changes in response to time-dependent variations of metabolite and hormone concentrations in the blood plasma profile. Model input was a generic diurnal plasma profile comprising carbohydrates, fatty acids, amino acids, and hormones. The simulation output is the metabolic state of the sample at any time point of this 24h cycle (i.e., the concentration values of all internal metabolites, internal fluxes, and exchange fluxes). Tissue oxygen uptake as well as the mitochondrial membrane potential were calculated.
2.10
Statistics
The distribution of variables was analyzed using the Shapiro-Wilk normality test and graphical methods (Q-Q plots). Variance homogeneity was determined with the Bartlett test. Continuous data are presented as mean and standard deviation (mean ± SD) or box plots including individual values. In case of normal distribution, ordinary three-way ANOVA and Fishers’ LSD multiple comparison post hoc test were performed. Application of other statistical tests is specified in the respective figure legend. p < 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance (* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001). Statistical analyses were performed with IBM SPSS Statistics Software Version 25. Graphical representations were prepared using GraphPad Prism (version 7.0, La Jolla, USA).

Introduction
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common type of primary liver cancer and the number of HCC-developing patients with underlying nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), the hepatic manifestation of the metabolic syndrome, is rapidly increasing. Considering the globally rising prevalence of NAFLD and particularly its stage nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), this raises international concern.
Therapeutic options for HCC are mostly invasive and include local ablation, liver resection and liver transplantation. However, despite advanced surgical procedures they are not applicable to most HCC patients. Conventional cytotoxic regimens are ineffective and even new combinations of immune checkpoint and molecular targeted therapies suffer from low complete response rates and are limited to advanced HCC
[1]
. Taken together, an urgent need exists to identify innovative and effective systemic treatments. The growing understanding of disease-driving signaling pathways and the consideration of differences between HCC etiologies hold promise to enable HCC precision medicine
[2]
.
Since the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) is upregulated in 40-50 % of HCCs [
3
,
4
], it has frequently been addressed in HCC-related research
[5]
. mTOR is comprised of two complexes. mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) responds to various factors (nutrients, growth factors as well as cellular stress and energy status). Its activation promotes proliferation, protein biosynthesis and lipogenesis while inhibiting autophagy
[6]
. mTORC2 is mainly integrating growth factor-dependent signaling into cellular metabolism, growth, cytoskeletal organization, and cell survival
[7]
. Growth inhibitory effects on HCC cells caused by mTOR-pathway blockade were repeatedly demonstrated for both first- (mTORC1) and second-generation (mTORC1/mTORC2) inhibitors. A study of our group using murine NASH-HCC-derived tumor cells demonstrated that a first-generation mTOR inhibitor (Everolimus) reduced cell proliferation only marginally. However, the second-generation dual inhibitor KU-0063794 resulted in profound and dose-dependent decrease of growth
[8]
, well in line with other preclinical data [
9
,
10
]. In contrast, the clinical use of these substances (e.g. Everolimus), showed merely low response rates
[11]
. So far, one crucial limitation of clinical trials on mTOR-inhibition in HCC treatment is the lack of considering the heterogeneity of HCCs. A distinguished focus on different etiologies such as NASH-HCC is likely to improve the outcome of targeted therapies.
To investigate the consequences of mTOR loss on the pathogenesis of metabolic syndrome-related HCC, we applied a well-established murine NASH-HCC model to a recently described liver epithelial cell-specific mTOR knock-out mouse strain (termed mTOR
LEC
)
[12]
. The aim of this study was to expand the knowledge on the impact and effects of mTOR-signaling in liver cancer with focus on metabolic consequences.

Results
3.1
Characterization of NASH-associated HCC
Figs. 1
C and D show representative µCT reconstructions and liver tissue images, respectively (see Supplementary Fig. 2 for results from all experimental groups). mTOR
WT
control mice (WT
(Acetone-SC)
) showed no signs of tumor development. In vehicle control mice that had received the western diet (WT
(Acetone-WD)
, mTOR
LEC(Acetone-WD)
) as well as DMBA-treated mice under standard chow (WT
(DMBA-SC)
, mTOR
LEC (DMBA-SC)
) we observed mild tumorigenesis. In contrast, all WT
(DMBA-WD)
and mTOR
LEC (DMBA-WD)
mice developed tumors. Notably, knock-out groups showed higher proportions of tumor-positive livers and significantly higher tumor load than the respective WT groups (
Fig. 1
E-G; Table S4). mTOR deletion efficiency and reduction of protein expression in isolated hepatocytes are documented elsewhere
[12]
. Assessment of mTOR expression in livers of DMBA-treated and western diet-fed animals was carried out via whole-tissue mass spectrometry proteomics analysis from tumor and non-tumor liver samples. The levels were found to be reduced to as low as around 20 % when comparing the non-tumor liver tissue of mTOR
LEC (DMBA-WD)
to WT
(DMBA-WD)
mice (
Fig. 1
H). Interestingly, the expression in tumor tissues from mTOR
LEC (DMBA-WD)
and WT
(DMBA-WD)
mice were not significantly different and much closer to the expression level in WT non-tumor tissue. Consequently, mTOR
LEC (DMBA-WD)
tumor livers contained around 4 times more mTOR than corresponding non-malignant tissue. Notably, staining patters of mTOR downstream target phospho-pS6 were similar in WT
(DMBA-WD)
and mTOR
LEC (DMBA-WD)
livers with higher intensities in tumors versus non-tumor tissue (
Fig. 1
I).
3.2
Scoring of NASH, fibrosis, and liver injury

(DMBA-WD)
and mTOR
LEC (DMBA-WD)
tissues are shown in
Fig. 2
A (for all groups see Supplementary Fig. 3A). As expected, WD feeding resulted in higher NAS-scores (Supplementary Fig. 3B). Focusing on the western diet groups, NAS- and SAF-scores were significantly lower in mTOR
LEC (DMBA-WD)
compared to WT
(DMBA-WD)
(
Figs. 2
B, C). Particularly, steatosis was less pronounced in mTOR
LEC (DMBA-WD)
tissue (
Fig. 2
D) and mild perisinusoidal fibrosis was detected in western diet groups (
Fig. 2
E). Table S5 and Supplementary Fig. 3 include all histopathological examination results. The proportion of mice with liver fibrosis tended to be lower in knockout animals (Supplementary Fig. 3H, I). Staining of collagen fibers revealed a similar trend (
Fig. 2
A, F). No significant differences were detected regarding leukocyte or macrophage infiltration in WT
(DMBA-WD)
and mTOR
LEC (DMBA-WD)
tissue (
Fig. 2
G, H), which is consistent with the NASH-scoring results. The liver-to-body-weight-ratio was higher in mTOR
LEC (DMBA-WD)
mice compared to that of other western diet-fed groups (
Fig. 3
A, B, Supplementary Fig. 4A-D). This is in line with the high tumor burden in these animals. Hepatocellular damage, as evaluated by serum ALT and AST levels, tended to be higher in knockout animals (
Fig. 3
C, D, supplementary Fig. 4E-L).

Tissue proteomics profiles
To elucidate the effects of mTOR loss on the expression of metabolic proteins and enzymes we performed a label-free proteome analysis using nano LC-MS/MS. Five biological replicates of non-tumor and tumor tissue from mTOR
LEC (DMBA-WD)
and WT
(DMBA-WD)
livers were analyzed respectively. After filtering the initial raw data, 4430 proteins were quantified. Principal component analysis showed a clear separation of the sample groups (
Fig. 5
A). We found significant differences between non-tumor and tumor tissue when comparing the expression levels of Hspa5, known to be highly expressed in NAFLD liver tissue and correlated with the disease state
[22]
, and Apolipoprotein A-I, which is the main protein of high-density lipoprotein and critically involved in hepatic triglyceride deposition (Apoa1;
Fig. 5
B). However, no or minor changes were detected in the analysis of the expression levels of typical liver proteins such as albumin (Alb) and carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase (CPS1) or ß-Actin (Actb). Strikingly, LDL-receptor, responsible for hepatocellular cholesterol uptake, is markedly downregulated in mTOR
LEC
liver and tumor tissue. We conducted pairwise comparisons using student's t-test followed by interaction and enrichment analysis utilizing STRINGdb. A network of mTOR and associated proteins was significantly higher expressed in WT tissue when comparing the non-tumor proteome of WT
(DMBA-WD)
to mTOR
LEC (DMBA-WD)
(
Fig. 5
D), while no significant enrichment of relevant gene ontology (GO) terms was detected. Comparison of tumor tissues revealed a distinct number of proteins involved in arachidonic acid metabolism to be downregulated in mTOR
LEC (DMBA-WD)
mice (
Fig. 5
C and Supplementary Fig. 7; GO:0019369 and KEGG pathway mmu00590). In contrast, the most prominent cluster within the proteins downregulated in mTOR
LEC (DMBA-WD)
non-tumor tissue belonged to the arachidonic and fatty acid metabolic processes (Fig. 5E; gene ontology access numbers GO:0019369 and GO:0006631, respectively). Although the same GO term was identified in both conditions (tumor: WT upregulated, non-tumor: WT downregulated), Cyp2c50 is the only protein present in both depicted clusters (
Fig. 5
D, E). Several proteins in this network are also involved in bile metabolism (Reactome pathway MMU-194068), secretion (KEGG pathway mmu04976) and cholesterol transport (
Fig. 5
F). They mostly showed deceased expression levels in tumors. Some of them were hardly detectable in knockout tumors. However, Cyp2a4 and Cyp2a5 protein levels were highly elevated. Taken together these results illustrate profound differences in arachidonic, fatty and bile acid as well as cholesterol metabolic processes between non-tumor and tumor tissue. The hepatocellular mTOR-knockout seems to critically impact bile acid and cholesterol synthesis and transport.

3.5
Model-based predictions of tissue oxygen consumption and mitochondrial membrane potential
Given the immense complexity of liver metabolism, we applied kinetic modelling to evaluate the magnitude of energetics deregulation and reprogramming in NASH and NASH-HCC tissue. We used the expression profiles of all detected metabolic enzymes to predict the tissue metabolic rates. As expected, the model predicts major alterations caused by mTOR-knockout. We compared the calculated oxygen uptake rate and the mitochondrial membrane potential during a 24 hours timespan. Restricted oxidative metabolism often observed in cancer tissue has been correlated with malignant aggressiveness
[23]
.
Fig. 6
A shows decreased oxygen uptake rates in HCC tissues, which is potentiated by mTOR-knockout. Accordingly, the model simulation revealed depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane in both cancers (
Fig. 6
B). These data are indicative for a decreased mitochondrial ATP production rate and often associated with elevated invasiveness
[24]
. In line with the experimentally observed disease progression states, loss of mTOR aggravates this effect in tumors. Interestingly, there are no or only small differences between the non-cancerous tissues of both genotypes.

4
Discussion
The mechanisms underlying NASH and NASH-HCC pathogenesis are complex and emerging insights substantiate them to be unique from those caused by other etiologies
[25]
. In the present study, we investigated the role of hepatocellular mTOR on murine NASH-HCC development. mTOR has been shown to regulate various processes during dysplastic growth e.g. regulation of hepatic inflammation, metabolism, insulin resistance, oxidative stress and autophagy
[26]
. Considering these multi-layered functions in liver disease and the interrelated systemic consequences, it is challenging to decode the effects caused by mTOR-inhibition mechanistically.
We observed strongly accelerated tumor progression in mTOR-knockout livers after DMBA treatment and long-term western diet feeding. In contrast, others demonstrated diminished tumor growth after chemical mTOR-blockade [
27
,
28
]. Augmented HCC-development caused by mTOR activation has also been reported [
26
,
29
]. An important difference between our approach of genetic inhibition and drug dependent blockade is the resulting coexistence of mTOR-expressing and low-expressing hepatocytes in knockout livers. Chemical inhibitors generate more uniform but also unspecific effects. Since mTOR is knocked out in our model from birth onwards and most phenotypical characterizations were conducted 34 weeks later, adaptive mechanisms may have emerged, which likely result in a different outcome than acute obstruction via inhibitors. Future thorough investigation of the tumor initiation and early progression phase in mTOR
LEC
livers will shed light on time-dependent consequences of genetic interference with this pathway.
In agreement with our data, Umemura et al. observed strongly potentiated tumor induction and progression in a murine NASH-HCC model with hepatocyte-specific mTORC1-inhibition. The mice developed increased liver tissue damage and fibrogenesis together with low-grade inflammation
[30]
. Based on seemingly conflicting results, Robert Abraham hypothesized that “too much” as well as “too little” mTOR-activity provokes liver injury and predisposition to cancer development
[31]
.
As described above, the mTOR expression was clearly reduced in mTOR
LEC
mouse livers. However, protein levels were not significantly different between knockout and WT tumors. This led to the hypothesis that tumors originate from remaining mTOR-positive cells in an mTOR-low surrounding supporting tumor development and progression. Cells with high mTOR-activity may have a growth advantage through potentiation of nutrient-dependent signal integration into progressive behavior. Inflammatory cells might also be causally involved
[32]
. However, we observed no differences in the levels of infiltrating inflammatory cells between WT and mTOR
LEC
livers.
Interestingly, despite long-term western diet-feeding mTOR
LEC
mice gained less weight compared to WT mice and NASH-scores were significantly lower. Accordingly, animals with highest tumor burden exhibited milder NASH-related symptoms than the control group. Based on the widely demonstrated mTOR activation in NASH and NASH-HCC
[33]
this was unexpected. Moreover, we observed improved glucose tolerance and reduced accumulation of visceral and subcutaneous fat in knockout animals. Impressively, there were no differences in body weight or fat tissue mass between mTOR
LEC
mice fed with either diet. The reduced NASH severity in mTOR-knockout mice might result from depleted fat storage capacity in mTOR-low cells [
34
,
35
]. Mechanisms behind reduced body weight and fat tissue gain as well as improved glucose tolerance remain to be elucidated.
To unravel metabolic alterations caused by mTOR-knockout on a broader scale, we conducted a proteomic(s) analysis of the tumor and tumor-free liver tissue. Focusing on the expression of proteins and enzymes that are involved in metabolic processes, we identified several abnormalities. Cyp2c29, Cyp2c50 and Cyp2j5, which are involved in arachidonic acid metabolism, were downregulated in mTOR
LEC
compared to WT tumors. This is well in line with reports showing reduced expression of these Cytochrome P450 family members in NASH tissue and during HCC progression [
36
,
37
]. Cyp2j2 overexpression protects against NAFLD development in high fat diet fed mice
[38]
. Dysregulation of the Cytochrome P450 pathways were observed to play important roles during adipogenesis and pathogenesis of obesity [
36
,
38
,
39
]. Wang et al. reported that low expression of Cyp2c family members is associated with reduced HCC patient survival
[40]
. The roles of Cyp2a4 and 2a5, which we found to be strongly induced via mTOR-knockout, are still under debate in the context of liver disease. Expression of Cyp2a5 is induced via high-fat diet feeding and reacts to the cellular redox status
[41]
. Interestingly, Cyp2a5
−/−
mice are more sensitive to diet-induced obesity and show exacerbated liver steatosis rates
[42]
. Therefore, Cyp2a5 might be causally involved in preventing excessive fat accumulation in livers of mTOR-knockout animals. The highly homologeous Cyp2a4 was reported to be strongly elevated in diethylnitrosamine (DEN)-induced HCC and to be involved in hepatic toxin response mechanisms
[43]
. A direct connection between mTOR, arachidonic acid metabolism and other functions of the particular Cyp enzymes in NASH or NASH-HCC has not yet been reported. Another depleted cluster of proteins in mTOR
LEC
tumors regulates primary bile acid biosynthesis. Cyp7a1 and Cyp7b1 were hardly detectable in some samples. These findings are in line with the published literature
[44]
. The level of bile salt export pump Abcb11 was also decreased in knockout tumors. García-Rodríguez et al. reported a link between bile acid metabolism and mTOR-signaling
[45]
. Likewise, the toxic accumulation of bile acids in the liver (cholestasis) has been associated with HCC-induction and increased progression
[46]
. The role of bile acid biosynthesis associated Cytochrome P450 family members during HCC pathogenesis and the influence of mTOR on their regulation are still under investigation. Additionally, low-density lipoprotein receptor (Ldlr), the main receptor for hepatocellular cholesterol uptake, had lower expression levels in mTOR-deficient livers and tumors. Hepatic Ldlr expression has immediate impact on blood cholesterol levels
[47]
and mTOR influences its expression on the transcriptional and post-transcriptional level
[35]
. Cholesterol is the essential precursor for bile acid synthesis. Accordingly, the combination of decreased cholesterol import with lower consumption for bile acid production and excretion might provoke cholesterol accumulation in the blood in mTOR
LEC
mice explaining the observed high serum levels. Whether these deregulations are solely compensatory or active drivers of tumor progression is currently unclear.
We observed multiple signs of metabolic reprogramming caused by hepatocellular mTOR inhibition that finally led to altered mitochondrial energy metabolism reported to correlate with disease aggressiveness. Loss of mTOR very likely has fundamental consequences on nutrient utilization
[48]
and - depending on the dietary composition - might have detrimental consequences for overall sytemic health namely promoting liver tumor initiation and progression. More detailed analyses of central hepatic processes and functions like glucose and fatty acid metabolism as well as urea production and ammonia detoxification in mTOR-knockout liver and tumor tissue are in preparation. Future experiments will give insights in consequences of mTOR-loss at earlier timepoints to expand our understanding on tumor-initiating processes. The reasons for our striking observation of less weight gain and fat tissue accumulation under western diet feeding, which is accompanied by improved glucose tolerance need to be addressed as well.
5
Conclusions
In this murine NASH-HCC model, the hepatocellular loss of mTOR aggravates HCC development, which is potentiated via western diet-feeding, but occurs in all observed experimental animal groups. We therefore conclude, that mTOR functions as tumor suppressor with specific importance under NASH-inducing conditions. Our work further highlights the importance of the etiology on the pathomechanisms behind HCC initiation and progression.
